csv-to-postgres-etl.title: Bad rows in the nightly CSV
csv-to-postgres-etl.instructions: About 0.5% of rows in the supplier's CSV fail validation (bad dates, missing ids). The business still needs the other 99.5% loaded by 7am.
options: Fail the whole load until the supplier fixes the file
Load the valid rows and write rejected rows, with the reason, to a quarantine table
Silently skip invalid rows
Load everything and fix the data in reports
why: Blocks the business on a tiny fraction of data; nobody gets the 99.5% that is fine.
Keeps the load on time, makes every rejected row visible and re-loadable, and gives the supplier a precise list to fix.
Data disappears without a trace: totals drift and nobody knows why.
Pushes bad data downstream where every consumer has to clean it again.

csv-to-postgres-etl.title: Re-running a failed load
csv-to-postgres-etl.instructions: The load crashed half-way last night. You need a strategy that makes re-running the job safe.
options: Append the file again; duplicates can be removed later
Load into a staging table, then replace the day's rows in one transaction
Delete the whole target table and reload all history
Re-run only the rows after the line where it crashed
why: Creates duplicates every time the job is retried.
Staging plus a single swap transaction is idempotent: a re-run gives the same result and readers never see half a load.
Correct but slow and risky as history grows; one failure can leave the table empty.
Fragile: line numbers are not stable identifiers and partial rows may already be committed.

python-data-cleaning.title: Missing customer ages
python-data-cleaning.instructions: 15% of customer records have no age. The marketing model uses age; finance reports average order value by age band.
options: Fill missing ages with the mean age
Drop customers with no age
Keep the age missing and add an 'unknown' age band
Fill with 0
why: Invents data and distorts both the age distribution and the age-band report.
Loses 15% of customers and their revenue from every report.
Keeps every customer, stays honest about what is unknown, and lets each consumer decide how to treat it.
0 is a real-looking value: averages and bands become wrong.

python-data-cleaning.title: Choosing the duplicate key
python-data-cleaning.instructions: The CRM export has duplicate customers created by repeated sign-ups. Emails differ only in case and spaces; names are often misspelled.
options: Deduplicate on the full row
Deduplicate on normalised email (trimmed, lower-cased)
Deduplicate on name
Deduplicate on the CRM row id
why: Rows that differ in any field (e.g. a timestamp) are never detected as duplicates.
Normalising the stable natural identifier catches the real duplicates without merging different people.
Names are not unique and are often misspelled: merges different people and misses real duplicates.
Each sign-up got a new row id, so duplicates all have different ids.

data-validation-pipeline.title: Where to validate
data-validation-pipeline.instructions: Orders arrive from three source systems. Bad data has reached the finance dashboard twice this quarter.
options: Validate in the dashboard queries
Validate at ingestion, before data reaches the shared tables, and record results
Ask each source team to validate
Validate once a month with a manual review
why: Every dashboard re-implements the checks, and other consumers still get bad data.
One gate at the boundary protects every consumer, and recorded results show trends and which source is failing.
Useful, but you can't rely on three teams; the warehouse still needs its own gate.
Bad data is visible for weeks before anyone notices.

data-validation-pipeline.title: Blocking versus warning checks
data-validation-pipeline.instructions: A check finds that 2% of orders have a NULL discount. Another finds duplicate order ids.
options: Block the load on both
Warn on both
Warn on NULL discounts (default to 0 downstream, alert), block on duplicate order ids
Ignore both until a user complains
why: Stops the business for a recoverable quality issue.
Duplicate keys corrupt every total; a warning is not enough.
Severity follows impact: a defaultable gap is a warning, broken uniqueness of the key is a blocking error.
Quality problems compound silently.

rest-api-to-postgres.title: Paginating a changing API
rest-api-to-postgres.instructions: The API returns customers 100 per page. New customers are inserted while you page through.
options: Use page numbers (?page=1,2,3)
Use the API's cursor (next token) or keyset (updated_after + id)
Request one huge page
Page until an error
why: Inserts shift offsets, so rows are skipped or repeated between pages.
A cursor or keyset position is stable under concurrent inserts, so every row is read exactly once.
Usually capped by the API and times out.
Errors are not a reliable end-of-data signal and hide real failures.

rest-api-to-postgres.title: HTTP 429 Too Many Requests
rest-api-to-postgres.instructions: During the nightly sync the API starts returning 429 after ~300 calls.
options: Retry immediately in a loop
Respect Retry-After, back off exponentially with jitter, and cap the attempts
Abort the whole sync
Run more parallel workers to finish faster
why: Hammers the API and extends the throttling.
Backing off is what the API asks for; jitter avoids synchronised retries and a cap stops endless loops.
One throttled call loses the whole night's data.
More requests make the throttling worse.

incremental-loading.title: Choosing the watermark column
incremental-loading.instructions: Transactions can be corrected days later; corrections update the row and set updated_at.
options: Use created_at
Use updated_at, with a small lookback window for late commits
Use the largest id loaded
Reload the last 7 days fully every night
why: Misses every correction, because corrections keep the old created_at.
updated_at captures inserts and corrections; a lookback catches transactions committed late, and upserts make the overlap harmless.
Ids don't change on correction, so updates are missed.
Works but wastes work and misses corrections older than 7 days.

incremental-loading.title: Applying corrected rows
incremental-loading.instructions: A re-sent transaction already exists in the warehouse with an older amount.
options: INSERT and let the unique key error stop the job
INSERT … ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE when the incoming updated_at is newer
DELETE all rows for that day, then INSERT
Keep both rows and pick the latest in reports
why: The job fails on every correction.
A conditional upsert applies the correction once, ignores stale replays and stays idempotent.
Heavy and risky: a failure between the two steps loses data.
Pushes deduplication onto every report.

sales-analytics-pipeline.title: Choosing the fact grain
sales-analytics-pipeline.instructions: Analysts want revenue by product, by store and by day, and sometimes per order line.
options: One row per order
One row per order line (product × order)
One row per day per store
One row per month
why: Products can't be analysed: an order has many products.
The lowest grain answers every question; daily and monthly views are aggregations of it.
Loses product and order detail forever.
Far too coarse for the daily questions.

sales-analytics-pipeline.title: Multi-currency revenue
sales-analytics-pipeline.instructions: Stores sell in EUR, GBP and USD. Finance reports in EUR using the rate of the order date.
options: Convert with today's rate in the report
Store the original amount and currency, plus the EUR amount converted at the order-date rate
Store only EUR
Ignore currencies and sum the numbers
why: Historical revenue changes every day as rates move.
Keeps the source truth and a stable reporting value; reconversion stays possible if rates are corrected.
Loses the original amounts needed for audits and local reports.
Adds euros to pounds: the totals are meaningless.

hr-analytics-warehouse.title: Tracking department changes
hr-analytics-warehouse.instructions: Employees move between departments. HR wants headcount by department as it was at any month end.
options: Overwrite the department on the employee row (SCD type 1)
Add a new dimension row per change with valid_from/valid_to (SCD type 2)
Keep only the hire department
Recompute from emails
why: History is lost: past headcounts move with each transfer.
Each version keeps its validity period, so any month end can be reconstructed with a date-range join.
Wrong for anyone who has moved.
Not a reliable source of organisational data.

hr-analytics-warehouse.title: Personal data in the warehouse
hr-analytics-warehouse.instructions: Analysts need headcount and salary bands. A few HR staff need individual salaries.
options: Give everyone the full employee table
Expose aggregated views and salary bands broadly; restrict raw salary columns to an HR role
Delete salaries from the warehouse
Share an export file by email
why: Exposes sensitive personal data to everyone who can query.
Least privilege: most users get what they need from aggregates, and access to raw values is limited and auditable.
Blocks legitimate HR analysis.
Uncontrolled copies of personal data.

star-schema-warehouse.title: Keys for the customer dimension
star-schema-warehouse.instructions: Customer ids come from two source systems that reuse the same numbers for different customers.
options: Use the source customer id as the key
Generate a warehouse surrogate key and keep (source_system, source_id) as attributes
Concatenate name and city
Use the email address
why: Ids collide across the two systems.
Surrogate keys are unique, stable and system-independent; source ids stay available for lineage and lookups.
Not unique, and changes when a customer moves.
Emails change and can be missing.

star-schema-warehouse.title: Do you need a date dimension?
star-schema-warehouse.instructions: Analysts filter by fiscal quarter, holiday and weekday, and the fiscal year starts in April.
options: No: compute everything from the timestamp in each query
Yes: a date dimension with fiscal period, holiday and weekday attributes
Store the fiscal quarter only on the fact table
Ask analysts to remember the fiscal calendar
why: Every query re-implements the fiscal logic, and holidays can't be derived.
Centralises the calendar logic once, so every report agrees, and makes filters simple joins.
Covers one attribute, and every new one needs a fact table change.
Inconsistent reports guaranteed.

pyspark-transformation.title: A skewed join
pyspark-transformation.instructions: Joining 2 billion events to 5 million users: one 'anonymous' user owns 30% of events and one task runs for hours.
options: Add more executors
Salt the hot key (or filter/handle it separately) and broadcast the small side where possible
Collect both sides to the driver
Repartition by a random column after the join
why: The single hot partition is still processed by one task.
Spreading the hot key across partitions, or handling it separately, removes the straggler; broadcasting avoids the shuffle.
Will not fit in driver memory.
Too late: the skew happens during the join shuffle.

pyspark-transformation.title: Output format for the lake
pyspark-transformation.instructions: Analysts query a few columns of very wide tables, filtered by date.
options: CSV
JSON lines
Parquet partitioned by date
One big text file
why: Row-oriented, no types and no column pruning.
Readable but large and slow to scan.
Columnar storage reads only the needed columns, and date partitions let queries skip whole folders.
Unsplittable and unqueryable at scale.

airflow-etl-pipeline.title: Making a DAG task safe to retry
airflow-etl-pipeline.instructions: The 'load_daily_sales' task appends rows; Airflow retries it after a network blip.
options: Disable retries
Make the task write the partition for its logical date (delete-insert or merge for that date)
Lower the retry delay
Add a sensor before the task
why: Hides failures that a retry would have fixed.
Writing exactly the logical date's partition makes retries and backfills produce the same result.
Retries still duplicate rows.
Doesn't change what the task writes.

airflow-etl-pipeline.title: Backfilling a year
airflow-etl-pipeline.instructions: A bug corrupted last year's daily aggregates; the fix is merged.
options: Run one giant job for the whole year
Clear and re-run the DAG for the affected dates (backfill), with limited concurrency
Patch the numbers by hand
Only fix data from today onwards
why: A single failure restarts everything and the code path differs from the daily runs.
Reuses the tested daily logic per date, can be resumed, and concurrency limits protect the source systems.
Unrepeatable and undocumented.
Leaves a year of wrong history in reports.

dbt-analytics-project.title: Materialising a large model
dbt-analytics-project.instructions: fct_events has 800 million rows and gains 2 million a day; a full rebuild takes 3 hours.
options: view
table rebuilt every run
incremental model with a unique_key and an is_incremental() filter
ephemeral
why: Every query re-scans the source: too slow for dashboards.
Correct but rebuilds 800M rows nightly.
Processes only new or changed rows and merges them on the unique key, keeping runs short.
Ephemeral models are inlined CTEs and are never stored.

dbt-analytics-project.title: Which tests protect a fact table
dbt-analytics-project.instructions: fct_orders joins to dim_customers and must have one row per order.
options: No tests: the SQL is reviewed
unique and not_null on order_id, a relationships test to dim_customers, accepted_values on status
Only a row-count test
Visual check in the dashboard
why: Reviews don't catch data changes upstream.
These encode the grain, the foreign key and the domain, so the build fails on the most common breakages.
Doesn't detect duplicates or orphaned keys.
Too late, and manual.

end-to-end-pipeline.title: Organising the warehouse
end-to-end-pipeline.instructions: Raw data from five sources lands daily; analysts need clean, joined tables they can trust.
options: Load raw data straight into the reporting tables
Raw (as received) → staging (cleaned, typed) → marts (business models)
One table per analyst
Clean the data in spreadsheets
why: Any source change breaks reports, and there is no way to reprocess.
Raw keeps an audit trail and allows replays, staging standardises once, and marts serve the business: each layer has one job.
Duplicated logic and conflicting numbers.
Unrepeatable and unscalable.

end-to-end-pipeline.title: Knowing the pipeline is healthy
end-to-end-pipeline.instructions: Last month the pipeline 'succeeded' for three days while loading zero rows from one source.
options: Check the job status only
Track freshness, row counts against expectations and data-quality results per source, and alert on anomalies
Ask analysts to report problems
Re-run everything daily just in case
why: A green job can still load nothing.
Data-level signals catch silent failures like empty loads and stale sources, close to when they happen.
Problems surface late and from the wrong people.
Doesn't detect the problem at all.
